title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 79
paragraphs: So when the armies had met in that plain in front of the city of Sardis—a plain wide and open, through which flow rivers (and especially the river Hyllus), all rushing down to join the largest, called the Hermus, which flows from the mountain sacred to the Mother surnamed “of Dindymus” and runs out into the sea by the city of Phocaea—then Cyrus, when he saw the Lydians being arrayed for battle, fearing their horsemen, did as Harpagus the Mede suggested. He gathered all the camels in the train of his army that were carrying provisions and baggage, took off their burdens, and set men upon them equipped like cavalry. Having thus furnished them, he ordered them to go in front of the rest of the army toward the horsemen of Croesus; and after the camel-troop he commanded the infantry to follow; and behind the infantry he placed his whole force of cavalry. When all his men had been placed in their several positions, he charged them to spare none of the rest of the Lydians, slaying all who came in their way, but they were not to kill Croesus himself, not even if he should resist when he was captured. Such was his charge. He had set the camels opposite the horsemen for this reason: because the horse is afraid of the camel and cannot endure either to see its shape or to scent its smell. For this reason, then, the trick had been devised, in order that the cavalry of Croesus might be useless—the very force with which the Lydian king expected most to shine. And as they were coming together to battle, as soon as the horses scented the camels and saw them, they turned back, and the hopes of Croesus were at once brought to nothing. The Lydians, however, did not behave as cowards on that account, but when they perceived what was happening, they leapt from their horses and fought the Persians on foot. At length, however, when many had fallen on either side, the Lydians turned to flight; and having been driven within the wall of their fortress, they were besieged by the Persians.
